title: The manners, reviewed

lines: A HAND ALL OVER THE PLATTER.
IT STAYED HIS WAY OF EATING.
cards: A boy sits at a shared platter of food in the Prophet's house.

He's the stepson of the Prophet, peace be upon him, and he's hungry, and his hand is everywhere: this side of the dish, that side, wherever the best piece seems to be. The Prophet gives him three short instructions.
Say the name of Allah. Eat with your right hand. Eat from what is in front of you.
That's all. In Sahih al-Bukhari, the boy, Umar ibn Abi Salamah, remembers it, and says, in paraphrase, that this stayed his way of eating from then on. Today, adab in everything.

teach.b: Adab, as the year defined it, is courtesy: toward Allah, toward people, and toward things. Not etiquette for show, but the shape a faith takes in small moments. It covers a lot of ground.

The year walked it room by room: the adab of speech, of eating, of guests, of travel, of sleep, of learning, of the road, of the market, of parents, neighbors and children, of animals and of the earth.

A single hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari holds three of them in one breath, in paraphrase: whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him speak good or keep silent, let him honor his neighbor, let him honor his guest.

In a report in Malik's Muwatta, in paraphrase, the Prophet says he was sent to perfect good character. So adab isn't an extra laid on top of the faith; that report puts it inside the reason the message came.
Back to the boy. Notice what made it stick.
The instructions were small enough to keep. Nobody handed him a book of rules. He got three things he could do at the very next meal, and he kept doing them.
That's how adab works across a whole life: one small courtesy, kept, until it's simply who you are at the table.

how: Muslims learn adab from the Prophet's example in hadith: saying bismillah and eating with the right hand, greeting others, honoring guests and neighbors, and speaking well or staying silent, and teach them to children at the family table.

o: a strict rulebook children memorize before they eat
polite table etiquette, kept mostly to impress guests
adab: courtesy toward Allah, people and things, in small ways

games.q: the manners, reviewed — tap the pairs.
p: with honor your neighbor and guest

s: the year defined it as courtesy toward Allah, people and things, the shape faith takes in small moments.
one hadith joins good speech, the neighbor and the guest
Sahih al-Bukhari: whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day.
the boy was handed a long book of rules
three short instructions, and he kept them for life.

games.q: you're the boy at the platter, reaching all over the dish. the Prophet speaks. what does he tell you?
o: leave the table until you learn.
say the name of Allah, use your right hand, eat from what's in front of you.
wait until everyone else has finished.
games.why: three short instructions, and in Sahih al-Bukhari Umar ibn Abi Salamah says that stayed his way of eating.

practice: Let the year's rooms pass by slowly, speech, the table, guests, the road, parents, neighbors, animals, and stop at the one nearest to your day.
Make it as small as the boy's instructions: not being kinder to everyone, but something like bismillah before lunch, letting the other driver in, or returning every greeting.
Choose one, and hold it for the rest of the sit, as if tucking it in a pocket.

wordCard.voice: The manners. Adab: courtesy toward Allah, people and things, carried into the smallest moments of the day. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: courtesy, good manners, the right way of doing a thing.

carryVoice: Your line: courtesy. Small enough to keep at the very next meal. See you tomorrow.
